hints: Notice each statement pairs accuracy or precision with random error or systematic error, so start by separating what accuracy and precision each describe.
Recall that random error causes scatter above and below the true value while systematic error causes the same shift in every reading.
Think about what happens to positive and negative deviations when you add several repeats and divide by the number of repeats, compared to a constant zero offset.
walkthrough: Identify the key terms: accuracy is closeness of the mean to the true value, precision is closeness of repeated readings to each other.
State the error rule: random error affects precision and causes scatter, systematic error affects accuracy and causes a consistent shift.
Check averaging: because random deviations are sometimes high and sometimes low, their sum tends toward zero when averaged, so the mean has less random error.
Check the contrast: averaging cannot remove a systematic shift because the same offset is present in every reading and so remains in the mean.

Apply this to the statements about accurate needing small random error and precise needing small systematic error, and about systematic error causing spread, and reject them as swapped definitions. This is option C.

options.A: Accuracy means closeness to the true value, which needs small systematic error, but readings can still be widely spread by large random error.
options.B: Precision means readings are closely grouped with small random error, but the whole group can be shifted from the true value by large systematic error.
options.C: Random errors are equally likely positive and negative, so averaging several repeats cancels much of the scatter and gives a mean closer to the true value.
options.D: A systematic error shifts all readings in the same direction, such as a zero error, while scatter about the true value is caused by random error.
